1 1/2 oz Balvenie 12 Year Scotch (Royal Brackla 12 Year)
3/4 oz Pineau des Chartentes (Guerin Blanc)
1/2 oz Benedictine
10 drop Housemade Bitters (1 dash Peychaud's)
10 drop Absinthe (St. George)

Stir with ice, strain into a coupe glass, and garnish with a lemon twist and an orange twist.
Two Mondays ago, I returned to the online recipe flashcards for Portland's Teardrop Lounge and picked the Sandcastles in the Sky from a section of old house originals. A 2009 Food GPS article cites Daniel Shoemaker as the creator and that it previously was made with Glenfarclas 12 Year Scotch and Floc de Gascogne (the Armagnac version of Cognac's Pineau des Charentes). The combination of Scotch, Benedictine, fortified wine, and absinthe made me think of Frank Caiafa's Tale of Two Roberts, and since the Benedictine and absinthe gave the build a bit of a New Orleans feel, I opted for Peychaud's Bitters here. Once stirred and strained, the Sandcastles in the Sky donated a lemon, orange, apricot, and charcoal aroma. Next, pear, apricot, and honey notes on the sip opened up into Scotch, orchard fruit, herbal, and anise flavors on the swallow.

content:
The agents, man. They’re everywhere.

At least 55% of deployments to Fly.io are now performed by agents. Bots passed humans in web traffic for the first time this year, mostly driven by the surge in agent use. Just a year ago, Cursor had 2.5x as many autocomplete users as they did agent users. In February, they reported that the ratio had flipped, with agent users now outnumbering autocomplete by 2x. We’re watching agent use transform our customer base in real time.

This isn’t a “trend.” Agents aren’t going to dramatically wane in popularity in a few years like sourdough starters. This is the new frontier, and companies are going to live or die based on how friendly they are to the idea that humans are increasingly one step removed from making product decisions.

We have to keep up here, for two reasons. One is that we have to stay in step with the market (we are, despite all this whimsical bird stuff, a business).

But the more important reason is that we just want to help you ship cool stuff; we try pretty hard not to have preconceived notions about how you do that, because being prescriptive is bossy and uncool. With my CEO hat on, I call it “meeting developers where they are.” So if we’re paying attention to the data, it’s telling us that (many) users want to work through agents completely, and that they do not want to be pulled out of a flow state to go be a human body and click some buttons.

Roger that. So, we shipped a couple things to try and meet that need.

Making the front door agent-sized

Agents can sign up for a Fly.io account now

Filling out sign-up forms is for people with time to burn. We now support auth.md, an open spec for agent signup. It’s a simple thing really, just a Markdown file that tells agents how to register. Ours is at fly.io/auth.md.

  1. Your agent asks you which email address to use, then registers with it.
  2. It sends you a link and a code. You open the link, confirm the address with GitHub, Google or an emailed link, and type the code. If you don’t have an account yet, you name it and it’s created right there.
  3. Your agent collects its own credentials for Fly.io and Sprites, and goes back to work.

The agent’s credentials are only valid for 24 hours, and it can renew them itself. They cover the apps, Machines, volumes, secrets, deploys and Sprites in your personal organization, but not your org’s members or billing. It shows up on your tokens page as “Agent (auth.md)”, and revoking any one of its tokens cuts off its Fly.io access immediately (Sprites access ends within 24 hours).

Agents can pay

When all you want is for your agent to get a job done, it’s really annoying when it brings its whole operation to a halt just to ask you to log in somewhere and pay $1 for something. Now there are two ways your agent can pay for things it needs, safely and under suitable human supervision.

Fly.io account top up

Firstly, your agent can top up your Fly.io account now. When your org needs more credit, your agent can buy it over the Machine Payments Protocol (MPP) without anyone opening the dashboard:

  1. The agent asks the credits endpoint for, say, $25 of credit for your org.
  2. Fly.io answers 402 Payment Required with a payment challenge for that amount. HTTP has kept that status code “reserved for future use” since the 90’s. Well, the future is here and it’s an agent with a wallet.
  3. The agent pays the challenge with Stripe’s link-cli, which turns it into a spend request. You get a notification in the Link app and approve it.
  4. Fly.io adds the credit to your balance, and it works exactly like credit bought from the dashboard.

The agent also has to say why it’s spending: the request carries a human language reason that you really should read before you approve. Amounts are fixed at $5, $10, $25, $50 or $100, and the agent authenticates with a Fly.io token that can be made to expire in an hour.

Spend from a Sprite

For everything that isn’t Fly.io, your agent can reach for the Link connector. A domain, an API plan, whatever you want your agent to just buy instead of ask for. It’s easy to use. Your agent in a Sprite asks for a specific amount to spend at a specific merchant and says why. You approve it in the Link app, and your agent gets a single-use virtual card capped at the approved amount. That card stops working after 12 hours. The Sprites gateway lets through only the calls needed to request and collect a payment, so the agent can’t approve its own requests.

A unified MCP server and agent-friendly docs

One MCP server gives your agent Sprites, your apps, Machines, volumes, secrets and Managed Postgres. You decide what it can touch in a browser, with no token to paste. Also, the whole of fly.io is indexed and optimized specifically for agents, so they can read the docs themselves (let them brag about how much faster they are at it, it’s all they have).

The Sprites ecosystem is all grown up

What started as a few Sprites Connectors for the most popular agents has become a serious toolkit for agents working in Sprites. Give Claude Code, Codex, Cursor, OpenCode, Hermes and more a real computer that you don’t have to be precious about. There are SDKs for 8 languages and frameworks and 61 connectors, which let a Sprite call the services you want your agent to use, securely. Whatever your agent runs on, and whichever toys it likes to play with, they are probably on the list.

We’re still a tool for devs

So we’re building all these agent doorways, trying to make it as easy as possible for people who want to realize the dream of never interacting with a UI again. (You’re missing out on a lot of cool purple buttons, but hey, it’s your journey.) Which: fun. Obviously we like building new whizbang stuff.

We’re also wondering (like everyone else) what it means for The Industry that we’re paving the way for agents to run so much of the research → analysis → selection → payment → deployment loop. What will happen as a result of everything going through an agentic bouncer before it reaches the devs we’re used to building for?

Two ideas

First of all: who knows, we’re no more clairvoyant than you are.

But we are, as a group, pretty optimistic, and we’re seeing some positive stuff: a closed agentic loop that lets people on either end of the technical capability spectrum effectively gain super powers.

We’re getting pretty close to people with zero technical background being able to build with actual autonomy. There’s been a lot of talk about this in the past year, but if you actually watched a non-engineer friend try to build their own product, there’s always a moment when the agent has to break the fourth wall and ask for an API key or something, and the whole thing grinds to a halt. That’s pretty swiftly becoming a thing of the past; if you can keep the entire process in natural language, you’re going to have people who can build cool things with no idea how it is getting done. We like this. We are pro people having competencies in other areas (like…healthcare, maybe? Or clean energy?) and not having to go through someone else in order to make their thing exist.

And obviously, experienced engineers are now able to punch orders of magnitude above their weight class. We had a call with a customer last week, a speed-scaling insurance agency for wealthy households, working on redefining what that looks like in an agentic world. Engineering team? Two people.

It’s the same story in our own workshops and pretty much every agentic tool we build for ourselves is happening in Sprites these days. Why wouldn’t we reach for a hardware-isolated, purpose-built computer for agents?

One of our favourite projects is our software factory. You give it a job (“fix this bug”, “tell me what this error means”) from its web UI, a Slack mention, or an alert from Sentry, and it sends the work down a line of agents. One researches the request and finds the cause, one makes the change, one uses the running product to confirm the change worked, one reviews it independently.

Each agent is just Claude Code on its own Sprite. The work order lives in code, so an agent can’t talk its way past a gate, and the whole flow ends in a draft pull request. Obviously the agents can’t merge or touch anything related to authentication, billing or production without a human thumbs-up.

The cool part (if you ask us) is the second loop. When a job finishes, a separate agent called the Scorer reads back through every step and grades the run against five criteria that live in a markdown file. The same things you’d nag any engineer about. Is every claim in the report backed by a command it actually ran? Would the new tests fail without the change? Did it do what was asked and nothing else? Did it burn steps rerunning the same failing command? Those pile up, and when the same criterion fails three times in two weeks, another agent goes looking for the cause and opens a draft pull request against the agents’ own prompts. That pull request goes down the same line as any other change, and a human decides whether it merges. Self iteration FTW.

Okay, Fine, Everybody In

Not to be cavalier/kumbaya about the whole thing, but our real job here is the same as it always has been: get out of the way and make it easy for you to build. It looks like that now means giving agents whatever they need in order to act as proxies while you spin a bunch of plates at once. Great! Climb on in, agents. There’s enough hot air balloon for everyone.

content:
When you’re working in an unclear situation — you have no clear guidance, or you don’t know what will help — the best course of action is often just to flail about. This sounds counter-intuitive. Wouldn’t it be better to be cautious and wait until you have a better understanding of what’s going on? Typically not.

This is definitely dangerous advice. Flailing badly is a great way to damage your reputation at a tech company. We’ve all worked with engineers who seem to have nothing but bad ideas, and who are constantly pushing one stupid plan or another1. But if you do it right, flailing about is the best and quickest way to get that understanding and become useful.

How to flail

How do you flail well?

  • Try a lot of different things
  • Pay very careful attention to feedback
  • Ruthlessly drop things that are not getting positive feedback

Trying a lot of different things is the key to the other two points as well. First, the entire point of flailing is to get direct contact with as many different bits of reality as you can. Think of yourself as a caveman learning how to use an iPhone: the first step is to just hit all the buttons and see what happens.

Second, you need to try lots of things because most of your plans will suck. You’re flailing because you don’t know enough to just do the right thing, after all. If you just try one thing, it will probably be a bad idea; if you try ten things, one of them might turn out to be good. Because you’re not equipped to judge which is which, you need to be extremely sensitive to feedback2.

Third, trying many things also ensures that you’re not over-invested in them. If you only have one plan, you’ll want it to succeed. If you have ten plans, you only care about one of them succeeding, so you can drop plans that are failing. Since most of your plans will suck, this is critical.

When to flail

Coincidentally3, there are also three types of flailing that most engineers will encounter.

The first is product flailing. When you’re working on a feature that doesn’t really have product-market fit yet, everyone is in a state of uncertainty. You will typically have some central idea about where the value is, but there’s a lot of room to wiggle (i.e. flail) around the margins. When I worked on GitHub Models (now retired) I built a lot of features or integrations that didn’t really work. However, one of those — allowing AI inference to run from a GitHub Actions token — was surprisingly sticky, and turned out to be the seed of “Continuous AI”. If you’re working on a brand-new product and you’re not flailing, you’re likely investing a ton of effort into ideas that were always doomed. Far better to flail around until you find something with traction, then commit hard to that.

The second is engineering flailing. Sometimes a system is so difficult that it’s hard to see where you’d even begin improving it: either it’s so tangled up, or it’s already so optimized, or it’s just so large and unknown. Some engineers like to sit down and carefully work their way through the entire system before recommending changes. I think this is foolish. Modern large software systems are too complex and are changing too fast to do that. Instead, I recommend making a bunch of speculative changes4 and just seeing how it looks (or how it performs). If it doesn’t seem like an improvement, drop it immediately; if it does, dig in and figure out why.

The third — the one most relevant to senior and staff engineers — is organizational flailing. Often I’m put in a situation where the problems are not technical: usually two teams aren’t talking to each other, or some team is unhappy and the director/VP isn’t quite sure why. What do you do then? Well, I recommend flailing! Just try a bunch of things that you think might help5: automate pieces of manual work, volunteer to take over tasks, suggest long-term plans that could conceivably make things much better, and so on. Most of these won’t be useful, but it at least shows that you’re trying, which can go a long way in situations like this. A note of caution: this is the case where it’s most critical to be sensitive to feedback. If you instantly drop some plan of action that is failing, you can build trust; if you miss that feedback and press on, the people you’re helping will start to point their anger and unhappiness at you.

Why call it flailing?

Why am I calling this “flailing” when it sounds like a sensible approach? Because it feels like flailing from the inside. Your manager will (hopefully) look at you and see a proactive engineer experimenting with solutions, but you will feel like you’re repeatedly failing: acting with insufficient information, trying a bunch of stuff that doesn’t work, and in general making a fool out of yourself. This feeling is normal, but you must ignore it.

The unpleasant sense that you’re flailing is one of the many psychological barriers6 you need to push through in order to be an effective engineer. Knowing ahead of time that it’s going to feel like flailing can help you recognize the emotion and treat it as a positive signal instead of as a sign you’re in trouble. So long as you’re sensitive to feedback and willing to instantly drop plans that aren’t working, flailing can be an incredibly effective approach to difficult engineering and organizational problems.

  1. Working around people like this is one of the cardinal social skills of succeeding in big tech companies.

    ↩

  2. Both from the people around you with more expertise and from reality itself (which plan actually lowers latency, increases user metrics, etc). Ideally you’re dropping any plan that isn’t getting “wow!” feedback.

    ↩

  3. It really is a coincidence. I tried to come up with a fourth or cut it down to two to avoid the appearance of symmetry but couldn’t.

    ↩

  4. AI agents help with this a lot. You can just ask for five different refactors and skim them to see which one is most promising, for instance.

    ↩

  5. If you haven’t done this kind of work much you might be thinking “why not just ask people what they’re unhappy about and fix it?” In my experience, situations where that is possible get quickly solved on their own, and situations where other engineers get parachuted in are ones where nobody can articulate what change they’d want, or where that change is impossible for other reasons, or where everyone disagrees, and so on.

    ↩

  6. Others include the valley of engineering despair, taking a position even when you’re uncertain, or shipping code that isn’t perfect. “Many engineering problems are actually psychological problems” is a recurring theme on this blog.

    ↩

content:
OpenAI have just released a fascinating graph showing the perplexity over time of all their released models:

Here are a bunch of thoughts I have about this:

Why OpenAI?

  • This is the most visibility we’ve ever had into the internal training metrics at a frontier lab
  • Releasing training metrics in the name of safety is a very Anthropic move, and it’s surprising OpenAI was the one to do it first
  • Perplexity must be measured against some specific dataset (e.g. all models will score basically zero perplexity1 on the string “AAAAAAA….”)
  • We therefore shouldn’t expect to be able to compare any similar data Anthropic releases with this data, except in terms of the angle on the graph2

Is perplexity a useful measure?

  • Perplexity is an unsatisfying metric because it only predicts how well the model matches some held-out text: i.e. it only applies to pre-training
  • For frontier models, the rumor is that pre-training is 50% or less of the total time and compute spent training a model; the rest is RL, which this perplexity data tells us nothing about the success of
  • If you believe (as many do) that pre-training creates capabilities and RL merely elicits them, then perplexity would actually be a useful metric for capabilities (and indeed it does seem to go down over time as models get better)
  • However, even if post-training does not add new capabilities, there are clearly other measures of capability that do not necessarily correlate with perplexity, like the ability to improve with chain-of-thought

What is surprising about the chart?

  • Very few models share the same base (i.e. have the exact same perplexity). It was a common rumor that OpenAI was post-training 4o and 4.1 into many of their models, but it looks like it was just o1 and o3
  • It’s interesting that 4.1 and o3 share the same base, given how great a model o3 was and how underwhelming 4.1 was
  • You can see the point where OpenAI briefly give up on making large pretrained models at GPT-4.5, which had similar perplexity to GPT-5.3-Codex but was far less useful

It’s unclear whether OpenAI chose not to pretrain further or hit some kind of internal scaling wall, but it’s interesting to consider the world where they could keep smoothly scaling on top of GPT-4.5:

  • You can see a real acceleration in perplexity loss from GPT-5.2 on
  • This contradicts the common wisdom3 that OpenAI (and other labs) have largely given up on pretraining and are all-in on RL. Clearly the pretrained base models are improving rapidly as well

What does this mean for alignment?

  • AI safety researchers have been asking for more transparency into metrics like this for years
  • However, I don’t really know how much it helps. If the idea is to watch for a sudden scary drop in perplexity, only OpenAI will be in a position to notice, unless they start releasing data about the perplexity of their unreleased pretrained models (the graph shows one, but they should continue to do this)
  • If the idea is for labs to agree on perplexity thresholds they won’t cross (as the post suggests), it will be important to get more detail on what precisely the held-out dataset is

Do the improvements in the graph match how strong the models feel?

  • You can see a huge jump from GPT-3.5 to GPT-4 (which is how it felt), then broad stagnation4 until GPT-5.5, then rapid acceleration
  • I personally did not feel a big jump with GPT-5.5: o3 and GPT-5.3-Codex were the “big jump” models for me
  • However, that could be because those models were better RL-ed into using chain-of-thought tokens well, or avoiding the sycophancy trap, neither of which would show up in perplexity metrics.

I wrote this post up as dot points because I felt like I had a lot of loosely connected ideas about this news. If you found this much harder or much easier to read than my other posts, please email me5 about it and I will write either less or more posts in this format.

  1. Zero log-perplexity, technically, which is the measurement in OpenAI’s graph. Perplexity approaches 1.

    ↩

  2. It would be very interesting if Anthropic’s data doesn’t show the same broad pattern of pretrains getting smarter, but I bet it does.

    ↩

  3. To the point where some people are doubting the validity of the data.

    ↩

  4. Except for GPT-4.5, which many people loved but did not feel particularly strong to me.

    ↩

  5. You can reach me on Gmail at sean.goedecke.

    ↩

articles.summary:
Cynthia went from a literature grad program to explaining C/C++ runtime error detection tools in about three weeks. Since then, she has co-authored six books, with the latest one an ambitious 6-month “weekend project”. That makes her the perfect guest for the show. I asked her all the questions that make writing so unique: how she ended up writing so many books, how she keeps going, what her writing process is, where her ideas come from, and much more.

The interview is structured around a big part of how to write books, getting ideas with note-taking, her editing process of sitting on it overnight, and how she uses AI for writing (or doesn’t). There are so many insights, here just three of them:

  • “Readers want to read your authentic words, not soulless grammatical perfection”
  • “I feel like thinking through an idea doesn’t ‘count’ unless it’s written down somewhere”
  • “Please don’t let LLMs homogenize it”

This is the second episode of «Show your Workflow», a written podcast format that tries to convey the craft of writing behind the writer, and I couldn’t be happier to have someone like Cynthia, who is so experienced. I hope you enjoy
articles.title: We didn't really want to write a book. But we wanted to write that book—Cynthia Dunlop (Show Your Workflow #2)

articles.summary:
Ladybird is an astonishingly ambitious project: a new browser, in 2026, with its own implementation of most of the key components - HTML parsing, CSS engine, layout, JavaScript, even WebAssembly. It still uses a few external components - things like HarfBuzz for text shaping, Skia for 2D graphics, ffmpeg for video, and SQLite for the things you do with SQLite. Everything else is part of Ladybird, or code brought in from Ladybird's even more ambitious predecessor project SerenityOS.

This morning the Ladybird project released their first alpha, which means you can now install the browser (on macOS or Linux) without having to compile it yourself!

I've been trying it out today, and it's very impressive. It feels fast, the UI is lightweight and intuitive, and most of the websites I've tried to load in it have worked as they should. It looks like this (showing my video-compressor tool):

Here's the process tree after I opened six tabs in one window and another
articles.title: Ladybird's first alpha release
